newsitem.title: TURKEY: Prospects for Turkey-IMF standby deal still cloudy.
newsitem.headline: Prospects for Turkey-IMF standby deal still cloudy.

text.p: Prospects for a stand-by or long-term accord between the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Turkey are still cloudy ahead of a scheduled Fund visit to Ankara, bankers and economy officials said on Wednesday.
An IMF team will arrive in Turkey on April 1 for the annual two weeks of consultations. The visit was earlier expected to take place in May.

"For the time being, we don't have any preparations for a stand-by accord," State Minister Ufuk Soylemez, responsible for the Treasury and privatisation, told Reuters. However he said the government would ask the IMF "to continue its support".

Turkish business executives and bankers have urged the government to implement an IMF-endorsed programme to improve the troubled economy, hit by high inflation running at around 80 percent and a public deficit around 10 percent of gross domestic product.
Members from the coalition government's Islamist wing, the Welfare Party (RP), have said the economy does not need implementation of a stand-by accord.

They say the government's 1997 economic plans, set up under a zero-deficit budget target, is sufficient to help the economy overcome bottlenecks that dragged Turkey into a financial crisis in early 1994.
In its recent visit in late October, the IMF team had expressed reservations on the feasibility of the programme and urged the government to adopt a comprehensive anti-inflationary plan.
"There is no substantial improvement in the economy since November. I don't see any reason that the IMF would change its attitude and support the same programme," said a senior private banker.
State Minister Soylemez, a member of the conservative True Path Party, said the central bank was studying a medium-term programme. "Details of the programme will be clear in April," he added.
After completing its talks in Turkey, the IMF team will draw up two reports -- a recent economic report and a staff report that will include projections about the Turkish economy.
Bankers say any negative comment about the Turkish economy from the IMF would increase Turkey's borrowing cost in the international market.
Recent downgradings of Turkey's rating to sub-investment grades by Moody's, Duff & Phelps, Standard & Poor's, IBCA and JCR, have already put the country's borrowing efforts under pressure.
But despite the rating cuts, prompted by the country's weak fiscal position and concerns over political uncertainities, Turkey is still planning to borrow in the Eurobond market.
Soylemez said the treasury mandated J.P.Morgan and SBC Warburg to arrange a five-year $250 million Eurobond issue in the first half of April.

He said the government's firm committment to speed up privatisation and reform the loss-making pension system as well as high central bank reserves and decreasing domestic borrowing costs enabled Turkey to raise funds abroad.
But some bankers and rating agencies say there are concerns that frequent political turmoil might make it more difficult for the government to take necessary economic measures.

A recent political row, which erupted after the military asked the government to take urgent action against Islamist activism, is seen to have calmed down. The row had fuelled fears that the coalition might be dissolved or go for early elections.

But political analysts say political tension may rise again in the near future unless the Islamist-led government shows the willingness to take the actions proposed by the military-dominated National Security Council.
